Just saw flurries and all I can think of is, at least I'm not in Boston, at least I'm not in Boston...

Anyways, my uncle keeps his plants and a few of mine at his greenhouse about 10 mins from my home.  I don't like having to drive there to see a few of my plants but the upside is he keeps the temps above 50F overnight this time of year.  Hence I get some great early growth like this:

 

Whereas mine at home in my small greenhouse which I keep above 32F overnight are slooooowly putting out some flowers and pitchers.    This has to be the toughest time of year.  Seeing so much potential but knowing we still got weeks of roller coaster weather (and some possibly late freezes to protect the plants from) before they start hitting their stride

S. leucophylla var. alba Covington Co, AL. Regarding the discussion about leuco genotypes that will do well in cooler weather, I'd try this one out! This is the first leucophylla trap out of all the leucos in the collection to develop! Other plants in identical conditions are just starting to emerge.

It has been in the 50's and 60's for the past several weeks, with nights in the low 30's thru 40's, so it's pretty surprising to see a leuco trap that's so developed. This photo is from maybe a week ago, the trap is just about to crack open today:

posts.body_html:
Well, now that I'm home, I might as well put up some photos of my outdoor carnivores coming out of dormancy. Because it remained cold for longer than normal (I mean, we had one freeze that was like 60 hours!), everything is coming out of dormancy a bit later than normal.

First up is a NOID sarr from California Carnivore's rhizome sale last year:

It's got red flowers when they open, and it's got 4 growth points on it.

Next is a sarr I got from this year's sale. When it came, I was worried because although I had 4 pieces with growth points, the majority of the rhizome had broken off from them! I wasn't prepared for there to be so many bits, so the growth points were potted up into small pots. One pitcher is already opening:



Fortunately, the chunk of rhizome is popping up a couple growth points, which is great! It's a big piece -- around 1.5-2" in diameter and maybe 6 inches long.


Last but not least, a couple photos of my seedgrown VFTs. They're going into their 5th year now. Last year at this time, they were just opening up traps 1" long, but the biggest ones right now are like .8". They flowered last year and gave a nice batch of seeds.


This seedling was set back significantly first by being a red VFT that grows slowly, but also by being uprooted by a racoon and losing 90% of its rhizome to dessication. Fortunately, I found it and nursed it back to health. It's a pretty plant that gets super dark red:


I've got some indoor plants, but they're not sarrs and the only VFTs are seedlings. Also, my new S. rosea isn't waking up yet. It looks pretty bad because its nice, greenhouse grown leaves took a bit of a beating from the cold. The growth point looks really, really healthy though. (And the Drosera binata seedling in the pot is waking up.)

I was working on cleaning up my flytraps today, basically trimming off the dead traps from last year so they don't shade the new growth. I have a lot of flytraps, five rolling carts, 27 6" pots per cart and multiple plants per pot. It's pretty tedious work but I must admit that I enjoy it, sort of in a masochistic way.  Anyway, I didn't think to take photos of the flytraps once I finished working on them but I did take a few photos of some of my sarrs this afternoon.

S. Purple Sparks. First pitcher of the season just opening up.

S. Leucophylla Red#3.2

S. Flava Cuprea 'Best Clone'

S. Flava Rubricorpora x Saurus. Phil Faulisi clone

Hey Calen, Your seedlings look great! It's going to be like Christmas morning when you finely go through them.  You're correct, I'm not using water trays. I decided to try top watering this season because I got tired of my pots flooding in their trays every time we have a thunderstorm or heavy rain. So far it's been working fine. I've been watering the plants once a day in the late afternoon so that the plants have more time in the wet soil overnight. Granted, our intense summer heat hasn't started yet but neither has our wet season. Once the wet season starts nature will do a lot of the watering for me. I'm cautiously optimistic and I'll see how it works out.
